strengths: While the results agree with empirical intuition that inductive biases in the model reflecting properties of the data should improve sample complexity, it is interesting to see such a result made crisp for vision models, and with specific focus on the locality and translation invariance properties of visual data.

The analysis is non-trivial and requires heavy notation; the paper does a good job at walking the reader through the intuition, proofs, claims, and findings, however much of the theoretical development is relegated to the appendix.

The authors theoretical analysis is quite unique in my opinion. To the best of my knowledge, the proposed DSD model is novel, and the derived lower bounds are enabled by taking the learning algorithm (gradient descent) into account. This is necessary since a learning algorithm can simulate CNNs with LCNs and FCNs. While previous works have established a sample complexity separation when assuming training with gradient descent, they used a data model which did not seek to capture translation invariance and locality.

Theoretical proof is provided regarding the sample complexity of FCNs, LCNs, and CNNs. The theoretical proof is built upon several tools like Dynamic Signal Distribution (DSD), network architectures given DSD, equivariant algorithms, minimax risk, etc. Overall speaking, the paper is well-organized and easy to follow even for general audience.
The relation between sample complexity and the type of network is interesting.
There seems to be real improvements over previous works.
This paper is well-written and provides very supportive technical details.
The authors introduce an interesting data model called DSD to represent real-world vision tasks; the task is straightforward and simple, making it suitable for theoretical analysis.
Additionally, this task exhibits characteristics of locality and translation invariance.
weaknesses: The main weakness in my opinion is step connecting the theoretical findings to practice. I would like to see numerical results demonstrating the derived theory under the DSD model (even if constrained to single hidden layer networks).
Minor point, but in notation it is stated that vectors are indexed at 1, but on page 4, \mu_i[(i-1)d:id] is indexed at 0.

The Local Signal Adaptivity (LSA) activation function is quite different compared to popular used activation function, like ReLU or more recent activation function. A better justification of using LSA could be provided.

From the proof sketch in section 6 and section 7, it seems that the sample complexity is dependent on what is the learning setting; authors could add more analysis regarding how the results will change given the learning setting of 'U ◦ DSD', and discuss whether there is a setting where the sample complexity of FCNs, LCNs and CNNs is similar.

The only downside I see to this work is the fact that there is no empirical result which supports the theoretic result; it would be beneficial to add empirical results of the predicted complexity versus actual observation.

Novelty concerns: the core insights appear consistent with Wang & Wu (2023); the paper's novelty over that work is unclear, and the chosen algorithm (only two training iterations) seems unconventional and perhaps too simplistic.
Regarding the model definitions, what is the reason for limiting the norm of w_i to less than one? This seems implausible.
What necessitates the width of your FCN models to be defined as k? Shouldn't the lower bound be applicable to any width, at least intuitively?
Concerning the proof outline for theorem 6.1, a more comprehensive technical elaboration would be beneficial, offering detailed technical justification given its novel approach.
